briefing.headline: You've been doing this. Now understand what you did.
body: You've already run brew install, cd, git push, and chmod +x. You got output. Some of it made sense. Some of it didn't. This module is about closing that gap — not by starting from scratch, but by pulling apart the commands you've already used and explaining what every piece actually does.

Type the commands yourself. Don't paste. The point isn't to produce output — it's to build a mental model of what's happening. The verify at the end of each step tells you what success looks like. Don't move on until you see it.

reference.title: Navigation cheat sheet
reference.content:
pwd            Where am I?
ls             What's here?
ls -la         List with detail, including hidden files
cd <path>      Change directory
cd ~           Go home
cd ..          Go up one level
cd -           Go back to previous directory

reference.title: File operations cheat sheet
reference.content:
touch <file>           Create empty file
mkdir <dir>            Create directory
mkdir -p a/b/c         Create nested path
cp <src> <dst>         Copy file
cp -r <src> <dst>      Copy directory
mv <src> <dst>         Move or rename
rm <file>              Delete file
rm -r <dir>            Delete directory and contents

reference.title: Path shortcuts
reference.content:
~ is your home directory (/Users/<you>).
. is the current directory.
.. is the parent directory.
- (with cd) is the previous directory you were in.

reference.title: Pipes and redirects
reference.content:
cmd1 | cmd2     Send cmd1 output as input to cmd2
cmd > file      Write output to file (overwrites)
cmd >> file     Append output to file
cmd 2> file     Write errors to file

reference.title: How to get unstuck
reference.content:
Ctrl + C — cancel the current command.
Ctrl + D — exit a shell or program waiting for input.
q — quit man, less, top, and most full-screen terminal programs.
Cmd + K (iTerm2) — clear the screen.

reference.title: "No such file or directory"
reference.content: Either the path is wrong or you're not where you think you are. Run pwd to check, then ls to see what's actually there. Tab-completion is your friend — start typing a name and press Tab.

reference.title: "Permission denied"
reference.content: You don't have rights to that file or directory. Don't sudo your way past it — that's how people break their systems. Stop and check: are you in the right place? Is this a system file you shouldn't be touching?

completion.headline: M1 complete.
completion.body: You can navigate, create, read, move, and delete from the command line. Next up: M2 — VS Code.

steps.title: Where you are, what's here
steps.body: Two questions every terminal session starts with: where am I, and what's in this directory? Two commands answer both. ls -la adds detail — file sizes, dates, and entries that begin with a dot (hidden files like .env, .gitignore, .github/). You've probably run ls or cd without knowing exactly what they return — run all three now and read the output before moving on.
steps.tryCue: Run all three. Read each output before running the next.

commandNotes.what: Print working directory — the absolute path of where the shell currently is.
commandNotes.when: A script failed with a relative-path error and you want to confirm what the shell thinks "here" actually is. Or you just opened a new terminal tab and aren't sure if you're still in the same project.

commandNotes.what: List visible files and folders in the current directory.
commandNotes.when: You just cd'd into a new repo and want to see what's at the root. Or a tutorial says "open the src folder" and you need to confirm the folder is named src and not source.

commandNotes.what: Same as ls, but shows hidden dotfiles and a long-format listing with sizes, dates, and permissions.
commandNotes.when: Looking for the .env file a README mentions but can't find. Or checking whether a repo has .github/ workflows. Or debugging a permissions error — the permission bits show up in the long format.

steps.verify: pwd prints a path. ls prints a list. ls -la prints a longer list including . and ...
whenYoullReachForThis: Cloning a new repo and trying to orient — pwd then ls tells you where you landed and what's inside
A README references .env.example but you don't see it — ls -la reveals it was hidden
Claude Code says it edited a file but you don't see the change — ls -la confirms the file exists and shows the modified date
A build fails because a config file is in the wrong place — pwd + ls confirms where you actually are

steps.title: Move around
steps.body: cd changes directory. ~ is home. .. is one level up. - is wherever you were last. You go nowhere without these four.
steps.tryCue: Run each line. Watch how pwd changes after each cd.
steps.code:
cd ~
pwd
cd Desktop
pwd
cd ..
pwd
cd -
pwd

commandNotes.what: Go to your home directory — /Users/yourname.
commandNotes.when: You're lost in some nested folder and need a known starting point. Also the answer when you want to cd into a folder in your home dir without typing the full path.

commandNotes.what: Step into a folder by name (relative path from where you are).
commandNotes.when: You just cloned a repo with git clone and need to step inside it before you can run anything. This is the move you'll do hundreds of times.

commandNotes.what: Go up one level to the parent directory.
commandNotes.when: You're inside src/components/ and need to run npm install from the project root. Or you cloned a repo into the wrong place and want to back out.

commandNotes.what: Jump back to the directory you were in before the last cd.
commandNotes.when: Bouncing between two folders repeatedly — say, project root and a sibling docs repo. Saves you from re-typing long paths.

steps.verify: Each pwd prints a different path that matches what you'd expect from the cd before it.
whenYoullReachForThis: Cloning a repo and stepping into it to run the install command
Jumping from your project root into node_modules or src and back
A README says "from the project root, run X" — you cd .. until pwd matches the repo name
Claude Code wrote a file in a subfolder and you want to inspect it
Switching between two repos that talk to each other (front end and back end) — cd - is the toggle

steps.title: Make a workspace
steps.body: Create a folder in your home directory to play in for the rest of this module. mkdir makes directories — the same command you'll use every time you start a new project, scratch a quick experiment, or organize files.
steps.tryCue: Run all four. End up inside the new folder.
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir mve-practice
cd mve-practice
pwd

commandNotes.what: Make a new directory with the given name in the current location.
commandNotes.when: Starting a new project before git init. Or carving out a scratch folder for a quick experiment so you don't pollute your home directory.

commandNotes.what: Make a nested path, creating any intermediate directories that don't exist yet. (Not in this code block — see the reference cheat sheet.)
commandNotes.when: Setting up a project structure in one command: mkdir -p src/components/ui. Or following install instructions that say "create ~/.config/something/" — the parent .config may not exist.

whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a new repo before git init
Scaffolding folder structure inside a project — mkdir -p src/components
Making a scratch folder to test something quickly without cluttering your real projects
Following a tool's install docs that say "create the config directory at ~/.config/..."

steps.title: Create files
steps.body: touch creates an empty file. Multiple files in one command — separate with spaces. It also updates the modified timestamp of a file that already exists, but you'll use it almost entirely to make new empty files.
steps.tryCue: Run all three. Confirm the files appear in ls.
steps.code:
touch hello.txt
touch a.txt b.txt c.txt
ls

commandNotes.what: Create the file if it doesn't exist; update its modified time if it does.
commandNotes.when: You need a placeholder file before opening it in an editor — touch index.html, then code index.html. Or you want a .gitkeep in an otherwise-empty folder so Git tracks it.

commandNotes.what: Multiple files in one command, separated by spaces.
commandNotes.when: Scaffolding several files at once — say, touch README.md LICENSE .gitignore when starting a new repo.

whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a project and creating the standard files in one shot: touch README.md .gitignore LICENSE
Need an empty file to paste content into from an editor — touch then code
Adding a .gitkeep so Git will track an otherwise-empty folder
A tutorial says "create config.json" — touch config.json is the fastest way

steps.title: Put content in, read it back
steps.body: Six small tools that combine constantly. echo prints a string. > redirects that output into a file instead of the screen — overwriting whatever was there. >> appends instead of overwriting. cat dumps a whole file. head and tail show just the top or bottom. This pattern — "run something, send its output somewhere" — is how most real terminal work gets done. You used >> in M0 to append the Homebrew PATH line to ~/.zprofile; this is the step that explains what that did.
steps.tryCue: Run all six lines in order. Read each output before moving on.
steps.code:
echo "line one" > poem.txt
echo "line two" >> poem.txt
echo "line three" >> poem.txt
cat poem.txt
head -1 poem.txt
tail -1 poem.txt

commandNotes.what: Print the given string to standard output.
commandNotes.when: Confirming a variable's value (echo $PATH). Or generating a quick line of text to pipe or redirect into a file.

commandNotes.what: Send the output to file, replacing whatever was in it.
commandNotes.when: Generating a fresh file from a command's output — git log --oneline > commits.txt. Dangerous when you mean to append: > silently wipes the file.

commandNotes.what: Append the output to file instead of overwriting.
commandNotes.when: Adding a line to ~/.zshrc or ~/.zprofile without nuking what's already there — like the Homebrew PATH line you appended in M0.

commandNotes.what: Concatenate and print a file's contents to the screen.
commandNotes.when: Quickly checking what's in a config or log file without opening an editor. Or piping a file's contents into another command: cat data.json | jq ..

commandNotes.what: Print the first N lines (default 10). -1 means just the first line.
commandNotes.when: Peeking at the top of a big CSV to see the column headers. Or grabbing the first line of a log to check what process started.

commandNotes.what: Print the last N lines (default 10).
commandNotes.when: Reading the most recent entries of a log file — the failure is almost always at the bottom. tail -f streams new lines live as they're written.

steps.verify: cat prints all three lines. head -1 prints only line one. tail -1 prints only line three.
whenYoullReachForThis: Appending a tool's setup line to ~/.zshrc or ~/.zprofile without overwriting it
Checking the first or last few lines of a big log file — head logs/server.log or tail logs/server.log
Dumping a config file to confirm what's actually in it before editing — cat .env
Capturing a command's output to a file for later — npm test > test-results.txt
Piping a file's contents into another tool — cat data.json | jq . to pretty-print JSON

steps.title: Copy and rename
steps.body: cp copies. mv moves — and a move within the same directory is a rename. There is no separate "rename" command in Unix; that's the same operation as moving the file to a new name in place.
steps.tryCue: Run all three. Watch how the file list changes.
steps.code:
cp poem.txt poem-backup.txt
mv poem-backup.txt poem-v2.txt
ls

commandNotes.what: Copy a file from source to destination. cp -r for whole directories.
commandNotes.when: Backing up a config file before you mess with it — cp .env .env.bak. Or copying a working component file as the starting point for a new one.

commandNotes.what: Move a file. If <dst> is a different name in the same directory, it's a rename.
commandNotes.when: Renaming a file (mv Component.jsx Button.jsx). Or moving a file into a subfolder (mv stray-file.md docs/) after realizing it's in the wrong place.

whenYoullReachForThis: Backing up a config or env file before editing it — cp .env .env.bak
Renaming a file when refactoring — mv old-name.js new-name.js (better than the Finder rename if you also want Git to see it as a rename)
Moving a misplaced file into the right folder — mv notes.md docs/
Copying a working file as the starting point for a new one — cp Button.jsx Toggle.jsx, then edit

steps.title: Delete
steps.body: rm deletes a file. rm -r deletes a directory and everything in it. There is no Trash. There is no undo. Read the command before pressing Enter — especially if it has wildcards or absolute paths in it.
steps.tryCue: Run both lines. Confirm the three files are gone.

commandNotes.what: Delete the named file permanently. No Trash, no recovery.
commandNotes.when: Cleaning up scratch files after an experiment. Or removing a file Git is complaining about that you genuinely don't need.

commandNotes.what: Recursively delete a directory and everything inside it. The dangerous one.
commandNotes.when: Nuking a botched node_modules before running npm install fresh. Or deleting a build output folder (dist/, .next/) when a build is acting weird. Read carefully — typos here cost you real work.

steps.trouble: If you ever type something like rm -rf / or rm -rf ~ — stop. Don't press Enter. Backspace it out. These commands wipe your computer.
whenYoullReachForThis: node_modules is acting strange — rm -r node_modules then npm install fresh
A build folder (dist/, .next/, build/) is producing stale output — delete it and rebuild
Cleaning up scratch files after an experiment so they don't end up in a commit
Removing a file Git is tracking that you genuinely don't need (then git add -u to stage the deletion)

steps.title: Wildcards
steps.body: * matches any sequence of characters. ? matches exactly one. They expand before the command runs — so ls *.txt becomes ls one.txt two.txt as far as ls is concerned. Lets you operate on groups of files at once without typing each name.
steps.tryCue: Run all four. Compare what each ls returns.
steps.code:
touch one.txt two.txt three.md four.md
ls *.txt
ls *.md
ls ?ne.txt

commandNotes.what: Matches zero or more characters. *.txt matches anything ending in .txt.
commandNotes.when: Listing or deleting every file with a given extension — rm *.log to clear out logs. Or moving every Markdown file: mv *.md docs/.

commandNotes.what: Matches exactly one character. ?ne.txt matches one.txt but not none.txt.
commandNotes.when: Rarer than * — useful when filenames differ by a single character, like image-1.png through image-9.png.

steps.verify: First ls shows only .txt files, second shows only .md files, third shows only one.txt.
whenYoullReachForThis: Deleting every .log file at once — rm *.log
Moving all the Markdown files in a folder into docs/ — mv *.md docs/
Counting how many TypeScript files are in a directory — ls *.ts | wc -l
Checking that a build emitted what you expected — ls dist/*.js

steps.title: Pipes
steps.body: | takes the output of the command on its left and feeds it as input to the command on its right. This is the move that turns a handful of small commands into a real tool. Most real terminal work is short commands piped together — list something, filter it, count it, sort it.
steps.tryCue: Run both. Each pipe combines two commands into one operation.

commandNotes.what: Send the left command's standard output as standard input to the right command.
commandNotes.when: Any time a command spews more output than you want to read. Pipe it through head, tail, grep, or wc to narrow down.

commandNotes.what: Show only the first 5 lines of whatever comes in.
commandNotes.when: Sampling a long output to confirm the shape before you process it — cat data.csv | head -5 to see the headers and first few rows.

commandNotes.what: Count lines (word count, lines flag).
commandNotes.when: Counting commits in a log, files in a directory, or matches from grep. Any time you want a number instead of a list.

steps.verify: First command prints the first 5 lines of ls -la. Second command prints a single number — the count of files in this directory.
whenYoullReachForThis: A log file is huge and you only care about the tail — cat server.log | tail -20
Counting how many TODO comments are in your codebase — grep -r TODO src | wc -l
Finding which files mention a string — grep -r "useState" src | head
Pretty-printing JSON from an API call — curl ... | jq .
Filtering git log output — git log --oneline | grep fix

steps.title: Processes and stopping things
steps.body: A process is a running program. top shows them live, sorted by CPU. Useful occasionally — but the skill you actually need every day is stopping a command that's stuck, hung, or running too long. Ctrl + C is the cancel button. You will use it constantly.
steps.tryCue: Open top, then quit it. Then start ping and stop it.
notes: Watch the list update for a few seconds.
Run ping google.com — it'll keep pinging forever.

commandNotes.what: Show a live, auto-refreshing list of running processes sorted by CPU. Press q to quit.
commandNotes.when: Your laptop fan spins up and you want to know what's eating CPU. Or a Node process seems hung and you want to confirm it's still alive.

commandNotes.what: Send an interrupt signal to the foreground process. Most programs stop cleanly when they receive it.
commandNotes.when: npm run dev needs to stop. A test runner is hanging. A curl request is taking forever. Anything that locked up the terminal — Ctrl + C first, ask questions later.

steps.verify: You exited top with q and stopped ping with Ctrl + C.
whenYoullReachForThis: npm run dev is running and you need to stop it before you can run another command — Ctrl + C
A test or build is hung and the terminal won't take input — Ctrl + C
Your fan is loud and you want to know which process is doing it — top
Claude Code is running a long task and you want to abort — Ctrl + C in its terminal pane
A curl or ping is producing endless output — Ctrl + C

steps.title: Environment variables
steps.body: Variables your shell knows about. $PATH is the most important — it's the list of directories where your shell looks for commands. When you type git or node, the terminal doesn't magically know where those programs live; it searches PATH. "Command not found" means: "I looked everywhere on PATH and didn't find it." This is also how Homebrew, nvm, and every installer make their tools available without you thinking about it. You already ran echo 'eval ...' >> ~/.zprofile in M0 — that command added Homebrew to PATH. This step explains what you actually did.
steps.tryCue: Run all three. Read the output.

commandNotes.what: Colon-separated list of directories the shell searches when you type a command.
commandNotes.when: "command not found" for something you know is installed — PATH is the first thing to look at.

commandNotes.what: Your home directory — usually /Users/yourname.
commandNotes.when: A tutorial says "put this in $HOME/.config/..." and you want to know where that actually is. Or a script is misbehaving and you want to confirm which user it's running as.

commandNotes.what: Which shell program is running. macOS default is zsh.
commandNotes.when: Your .zshrc isn't loading and you suspect you're actually on bash. Or a tool says "add this to your shell config" and you need to know which file to edit.

steps.verify: All three print a value. $HOME matches your home directory. $SHELL is /bin/zsh.
whenYoullReachForThis: A command works in one terminal window but not another — different shells loaded different PATH values
brew install succeeds but the new command isn't found — the install didn't update PATH
A script runs locally but fails in CI — CI's PATH is minimal and missing something
Switching Node versions with nvm — nvm rewrites PATH every time
Claude Code says it can't find a tool you just installed — close and reopen the terminal so PATH reloads

steps.title: Get help
steps.body: man <command> opens the manual page. <command> --help prints a quick summary. When you forget what a flag does, this is the answer — not Google, not a tab in your browser. The docs are on your machine, offline, and they're the authoritative source.
steps.tryCue: Open the ls man page, then quit it.
notes: Scroll with arrow keys or space bar.
Search inside the page with / followed by your search term, then Enter.

commandNotes.what: Open the manual page for a command in a scrollable viewer. Press q to quit.
commandNotes.when: You half-remember a flag and want to confirm the exact name — man ls for the -la options, man grep for the recursive flag.

commandNotes.what: Print a short usage summary directly to the terminal. Faster than man for a quick refresher.
commandNotes.when: You want a one-screen reminder of subcommands and flags without opening a pager — git --help, npm --help, brew --help.

steps.verify: You opened the man page for ls and quit it with q.
whenYoullReachForThis: You forgot which flag is recursive — man grep or grep --help
A command isn't doing what you expected and you want to check the exact behavior before guessing
Claude Code suggests a flag and you want to verify it exists before running it
A blog post from 2017 uses a flag that may have changed — man shows what your version actually supports

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the practice directory. You're back to a clean home directory.
steps.tryCue: Run all three. The last command should error — that's success.
steps.verify: Final ls errors with No such file or directory — because the directory is gone. That's the success state.
